source.book: Tajweed Rules of the Qur'an — Part One
source.verification: book source checked; Qur'anic references cross-checked

prerequisites: Recognize the three forms of tanween: ً ٍ ٌ.
Know that throat letters come from three areas of the throat.
learningOutcomes: Name and recognize the six throat letters: ء ه ع ح غ خ.
Find the target and the immediately following letter.
Identify izhar in at least 8 of 10 examples and explain why.
Recite six guided examples with a clear noon sound, without merging or added ghunnah.

keyTerms.en: an extra noon sound at the end of a noun when continuing

teacherPreparation: Open page 41 of the source book.
Prepare the six throat-letter cards: ء ه ع ح غ خ.
Share only the lesson area on screen and reveal explanations after the learner predicts.
Model every Qur'anic phrase live; the interface does not replace teacher correction.

openingReview.teacherPrompt: Ask the learner to select noon saakinah from نَ، نْ، نُ.
Ask the learner to recognize the three tanween signs.
Ask: Which part of the mouth produces ء ه ع ح غ خ?

conceptExplanation.text: Look for noon saakinah or tanween, then inspect only the next letter. If it is one of the six throat letters, keep the noon sound clear. Do not merge it into the next letter and do not stretch a ghunnah.
Izhar means clarity. It occurs when noon saakinah or tanween is followed immediately by ء ه ع ح غ خ. It may occur inside one word or between two words.

linguistic.en: Linguistically, izhar means clarity and making something clear.

technical.ar: الإظهار اصطلاحًا: إخراج النون الساكنة أو التنوين من مخرجهما بوضوح، من غير إدغام ولا إخفاء، ومن غير غنة زائدة، إذا جاء بعدهما أحد حروف الحلق الستة: ء ه ع ح غ خ.
technical.en: In Tajweed, izhar is pronouncing noon saakinah or tanween clearly from its articulation point, without merging or hiding it and without added ghunnah, when followed by one of the six throat letters: ء ه ع ح غ خ.

studentFriendly.ar: ابحث عن النون الساكنة أو التنوين، ثم انظر إلى الحرف التالي مباشرة. إذا كان حرفًا حلقيًا، أظهر صوت النون بوضوح.
studentFriendly.en: Find noon saakinah or tanween and look at the very next letter. If it is a throat letter, keep the noon sound clear.

definition.memoryFormula: نْ أو تنوين + حرف حلقي = إظهار واضح

ruleSummary.condition: Noon saakinah or tanween is immediately followed by a throat letter.
ruleSummary.result: Pronounce the noon sound clearly, without merging and without added ghunnah.
ruleSummary.location: It can occur inside one word or across two words.

quranExamples.readingInstruction: Complete the noon clearly, then begin the hamzah separately.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is hamzah, from the deepest throat.
quranExamples.commonError: Dropping the noon or stretching a nasal sound.

quranExamples.readingInstruction: Keep the noon distinct before moving gently to ha.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is ha, from the deepest throat.
quranExamples.commonError: Weakening the noon before the soft ha.

quranExamples.readingInstruction: Complete the noon clearly before moving to ayn.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is ayn, from the middle throat.
quranExamples.commonError: Moving early to ayn and weakening the noon.

quranExamples.readingInstruction: Make the noon clear inside the word, then pronounce ha from the middle throat.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is ha ح, and izhar occurs here inside one word.
quranExamples.commonError: Hiding the noon because both letters occur in one word.

quranExamples.arabic: وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ
quranExamples.readingInstruction: Finish the noon clearly before moving to ghayn.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is ghayn, from the closest part of the throat.
quranExamples.commonError: Merging the noon into the heavy ghayn.

quranExamples.readingInstruction: Keep the noon clear, then pronounce kha without pulling the noon toward it.
quranExamples.teacherExplanation: The next letter is kha, from the closest part of the throat.
quranExamples.commonError: Letting the strength of kha hide the noon.

guidedPractice.teacherAction: Display only the target and following letter.
guidedPractice.studentAction: Name the target, the next letter, and its throat pair.
guidedPractice.feedback: Do not accept only the rule name; require the reason.

guidedPractice.teacherAction: Reveal the full phrase and model it once.
guidedPractice.studentAction: Point, isolate, connect, then recite the phrase.
guidedPractice.feedback: Correct clarity and unwanted nasalization separately.

interactiveActivities.prompt: Choose the noon that has no vowel.
interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The sukoon shows that the noon has no vowel.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the small sukoon sign above the noon.

instruction.en: Which group contains all three tanween signs?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. These three endings produce an extra noon sound when continuing.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Tanween is written with doubled vowel signs.

instruction.en: Where are the six izhar letters articulated?

interactiveActivities.prompt: ء ه ع ح غ خ
interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. They are the six throat letters.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Say the letters slowly and notice where their sound begins.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Hamzah is the letter immediately after noon saakinah.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: First find نْ, then inspect only the next letter.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ha ه follows noon saakinah.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The trigger is the letter immediately after نْ.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ayn is a middle-throat letter.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Look immediately after noon saakinah.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ha ح follows noon saakinah inside the word.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Izhar can also occur inside one word.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ghayn is a closest-throat letter.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Find the first letter after نْ.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Kha is one of the six throat letters.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The trigger comes directly after noon saakinah.

instruction.en: Which pair comes from the deepest throat?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Hamzah and ha come from the deepest throat.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Remember the pairs from deep to near: ء ه · ع ح · غ خ.

instruction.en: Which pair comes from the middle throat?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ayn and ha ح come from the middle throat.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The middle pair is ع ح.

instruction.en: Which pair comes from the closest part of the throat?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ghayn and kha are the closest-throat pair.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The pair nearest the mouth is غ خ.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Noon saakinah is followed by ayn.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Ayn is one of the six throat letters.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Noon saakinah is followed by kha.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Kha belongs to the throat group.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Ya is not one of the six izhar letters.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Check the next letter against ء ه ع ح غ خ.

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Mim is not a throat letter.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The next letter is mim, not one of ء ه ع ح غ خ.

instruction.en: A learner merges the noon into ayn. What should change?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Complete the noon, then move separately to ayn.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Izhar means clarity; the noon must remain audible.

instruction.en: A learner holds a long nasal sound before kha. What is the correction?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Keep the noon clear without prolonging nasalization.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The clear noon is not merged or given an added ghunnah.

instruction.en: A learner says izhar cannot occur inside one word. Which example corrects that idea?

interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. In وَٱنْحَرْ, noon saakinah and ح are in the same word.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Look for نْ and the throat letter inside a single word.

interactiveActivities.prompt: Noon saakinah or tanween + a throat letter = …
interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. This is the full izhar condition.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: The noon remains clear when a throat letter follows.

instruction.en: Which answer gives the complete reason?

items: Because ghayn follows noon saakinah and ghayn is a throat letter
acceptedAnswers: Because ghayn follows noon saakinah and ghayn is a throat letter
interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Excellent. You named the target, the following letter, and its group.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: A complete reason names the target, the next letter, and why that letter triggers izhar.

interactiveActivities.prompt: How should the noon sound be read in إِنْ هُوَ?
interactiveActivities.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Now recite it to your teacher.
interactiveActivities.feedbackIncorrect: Izhar keeps the noon sound clear.

commonMistakes: Adding a prolonged ghunnah to the clear noon.
Weakening or dropping the noon sound.
Merging the noon into the following throat letter.
Looking at a later letter instead of the immediately following letter.
Thinking izhar occurs only between two words.
correctionTechniques: Isolate noon with sukoon, pronounce the throat letter separately, then reconnect them.
Point to the exact boundary and ask: What comes immediately after the noon sound?
Use the three pairs ء ه · ع ح · غ خ instead of memorizing an unstructured six-letter list.
Require the learner to recite after every recognition answer.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Name the six izhar letters and group them by the three throat areas.
knowledgeChecks.success: All six letters are named and grouped correctly.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Classify ten mixed noon-saakinah and tanween boundaries.
knowledgeChecks.success: At least eight are identified correctly with a reason.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Recite one example for each throat letter.
knowledgeChecks.success: The noon remains clear without merging or added ghunnah.

What letter comes immediately after it?
Is that letter one of ء ه ع ح غ خ?
How should the noon sound be recited?

Highlight the target and trigger in every phrase.
Recite one example for each of the six letters.

independentPractice: Review the six letters as three pairs: ء ه · ع ح · غ خ.
For each assigned phrase, mark the target, circle the trigger, name the rule, then recite.
homework: Prepare three teacher-approved examples: identify the trigger, explain the rule, then recite.
Do not self-certify pronunciation; bring the reading back for teacher correction.
exitTicket: Recognition: identify the target and trigger in مِنْ غِلٍّ.
Explanation: say why izhar applies using a complete sentence.
Oral task: recite one teacher-selected example clearly.
masteryCriteria: Names all six throat letters and groups them into three pairs.
Identifies izhar in at least 8 of 10 mixed boundaries.
Explains each answer by naming the following throat letter.
Recites one example for each letter without merging or added prolonged ghunnah.
Correctly diagnoses the three common errors in this lesson.
teacherNotes: Use one decision routine throughout: target → next letter → throat group → rule → recitation.
Do not move through all activities in silence; after recognition, ask the learner to recite.
Knowledge of the six letters does not equal recitation mastery.
Supplementary examples were added to provide one verified example for every throat letter; page 41 remains the primary book source.
Teacher script: The next letter is from the throat, so keep the noon clear, then move to the next letter without merging or added ghunnah.
